conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. Thank you for making time to talk today; caring for a new baby is exhausting and you’re doing something important for yourself by being here.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past seven days. The answers will give us a snapshot of mood, anxiety, and stress that can show up after childbirth, and they’ll guide us toward the best support for you.

Everything you share stays confidential within our clinical team. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. It’s simply ten questions; most moms finish in just a few minutes.

Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft exhale]  
Honestly… most of the time it feels kind of forced. My sister sent me a silly video yesterday and I managed a little laugh, but it disappeared right away—like I can’t hold on to that light feeling any more. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
Not really… I mean, I *can* laugh a little, but it’s like I’m pretending most of the time. Nothing feels truly funny the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to the floor]  
Not much… I still get a spark when I think about maybe grabbing coffee with my best friend, but it’s pretty dim. Most stuff I used to count on for a boost—like a walk with the stroller or even online shopping—just feels like another chore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If he spits up more than usual or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I keep replaying little moments and thinking a better mom would’ve known how to fix it. It’s not every second, but it’s been happening several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[fidgets with the edge of the baby blanket]  
Pretty much, yeah. I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly my chest feels tight—like something awful’s about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. I keep checking if he’s breathing in the bassinet, and every little noise outside makes my heart race. There isn’t always a clear reason; the worry just shows up and sticks around.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands]  
Twice this week it hit me out of nowhere—my heart started racing, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to put the baby in the crib so I could sit on the floor and hug my knees. It felt like the room was closing in, even though nothing dangerous was happening. It passes after a few minutes, but I’m left shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]  
Yes… most days it feels like the dishes, the laundry, the texts I haven’t answered, the night feeds—they all pile up faster than I can touch them. I’ll start one chore and end up staring at the wall feeling like I’m drowning. I’m not falling apart completely, but I keep thinking, “I can’t keep up with any of this.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
Yeah… I lie down right after I put him in the bassinet, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I wash the bottles, is he breathing, am I already failing him? It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I wake up at least once or twice with my heart pounding and those same worries. Even when the baby’s asleep, I’m not really resting.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes welling]  
Most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding him and just start tearing up for no clear reason. I keep thinking, “I should be grateful,” but the sadness is just… there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, voice cracks]  
Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I was folding his tiny onesies and suddenly felt like I’m failing him; the tears just started rolling and I couldn’t stop them for almost ten minutes. It’s not every single day, but when it hits, it feels overwhelming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, eyes on lap]  
...Once or twice, but it’s more like a scary flash than a plan. I’ll be rocking him at 3 a.m. and out of nowhere think, “What if I just disappeared?” It scares me so much I squeeze him tighter and push it away. I don’t want to die—I just want the hurting to stop.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived-laughter feels forced, simple pleasures now feel like chores, and a persistent gray cloud of sadness hangs over most days. You're blaming yourself whenever anything seems "off" with your little one, and sudden waves of worry or even panic take your breath away, especially when the house feels like it's closing in. Nights are long; your mind races with "what-ifs," making real rest almost impossible, and you've found yourself in tearful moments that seem to come from nowhere. Most frightening of all, brief flashes of wishing you could "just disappear" have surfaced, though you quickly push them aside because you want to be here for your child. What you're experiencing is not a personal failing-it's a very real, treatable set of postpartum mood symptoms, and you deserve support that helps the hurting stop.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to feel genuine amusement, describing laughter as pretense and loss of prior joy, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—only a "dim spark" for one activity and loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed tasks—matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame multiple times daily, aligning with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes frequent, intense anxiety with physical symptoms (tight chest, racing heart) that occur "very often" without clear triggers.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense episodes of panic (racing heart, breathlessness, room closing in) occurring twice this week without identifiable cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily tasks piling up, feeling overwhelmed ('drowning'), inability to cope with routine chores, and persistent thought 'I can't keep up', indicating significant impairment matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the day, every day" with uncontrollable crying spells, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear tearful episodes twice in the past week with intense distress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, unwanted thoughts of self-harm occurring once or twice, fitting "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> in almost all activities, <sym>fatigue</sym> described as feeling overwhelmed, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym> and excessive guilt, and recurrent <sym>passive suicidal thoughts</sym> without intent. She also describes discrete panic symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea, fear of impending doom) meeting criteria for co-occurring <med>panic attacks</med>. Symptom onset within four weeks postpartum aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss these results and safety planning
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place; remove or secure any potentially harmful items as a precaution
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or your local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel you might act on them
4. Schedule a formal evaluation with a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for diagnosis and to discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
5. Aim for short, manageable self-care moments: five-minute shower, a single glass of water, or opening the curtains for daylight; small steps count
6. Consider peer support-local or online <med>postpartum support groups</med> can reduce isolation and provide practical tips
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant present)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [licensed MHP]

A. Key symptoms endorsed  
- Depressed mood, tearfulness most of the day, nearly daily  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia) for both social and routine activities  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“several × daily”)  
- Psychomotor anxiety: racing heart, startle response, repeated infant-checking  
- Two episodes this week of sudden panic (palpitations, dyspnea, need to set baby down)  
- Sleep-onset and mid-night awakening linked to intrusive worries  
- Sense of being overwhelmed / unable to keep up with daily tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“What if I just disappeared?”) without plan or intent; patient reports fear of the thought and immediate efforts to suppress

B. Pattern summary  
Symptoms cluster around persistent low mood, anxiety, and self-criticism, with functional impact on sleep, self-care, and parenting confidence. No current psychotic features or substance indicators reported. Protective factors: strong desire to care for infant, no active self-harm plan, willing to engage in help-seeking.

C. Screening significance / differential flags  
- Meets threshold for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset  
- Co-occurring panic attacks / generalized anxiety  
- Passive suicidal ideation → elevated safety risk requiring formal risk assessment and safety-planning

D. Recommendations (screening level)  
1. Same-day formal diagnostic interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS, plus suicide risk probe).  
2. Coordinate with OB/midwife and PCP; consider expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry.  
3. Provide 24-hr crisis line, remove lethal means, develop safety plan with supports.  
4. Psycho-education on postpartum mood/anxiety disorders and treatment options.

End of screening note.
